elements.id-string-3: Clickbait is the practice of engineering titles to incentivize readers to click through to articles.
elements.id-string-4: Such titles with sensationalized language reveal as little information as possible.
elements.id-string-5: Occasionally, clickbait will be intentionally misleading, so natural language processing (NLP) can scan the article and answer the question posed by the clickbait title, or spoil it.
elements.id-string-6: We tackle two tasks: classifying the clickbait into one of 3 types (Task 1), and spoiling the clickbait (Task 2).
elements.id-string-7: For Task 1, we propose two binary classifiers to determine the final spoiler type.
elements.id-string-8: For Task 2, we experiment with two  approaches: using a question-answering model to identify the span of text of the spoiler, and using a large language model (LLM) to generate the spoiler.
elements.id-string-9: Because the spoiler is contained in the article, we frame the second task as a question-answering approach for identifying the starting and ending positions of the spoiler.
elements.id-string-10: We created models for Task 1 that were better than the baselines proposed by the dataset authors and engineered prompts for Task 2 that did not perform as well as the baselines proposed by the dataset authors due to the evaluation metric performing worse when the output text is from a generative model as opposed to an extractive model.
elements.id-string-12: It is an issue that plagues the internet, and spreads disinformation while causing readers to go through extreme methods to find the real content of an article.
elements.id-string-13: Many people, however, may not go to such an extent to find answers and will instead believe misleading information in the clickbait titles.
elements.id-string-14: Effectively, many may "judge a book by its cover." Such a problem can be solved by "adding to the cover" and creating a natural language processing model to "spoil" the article and reveal a short summary which answers the question posed by the clickbait title.
elements.id-string-15: We tackle two tasks that can help with the spoiling clickbait.
elements.id-string-16: Task 1 is classification, where the data is split into three categories to make the next task easier.
elements.id-string-17: Task 2 is spoiling, where we reveal the answer to the title.
elements.id-string-18: Task 1 makes Task 2 much easier because we can develop multiple algorithms to tackle the multiple types of clickbait.

elements.id-string-28: We obtain our dataset from a shared task called SemEval.
elements.id-string-29: SemEval is a group and runs 12 tasks per year; we used the dataset from the Clickbait shared task.
elements.id-string-30: Specifically, the organizers of our tasks published a paper in which they defined a task, created a dataset, and made baseline classifiers.
elements.id-string-31: \cite{hagen_frobe_jurk_potthast_2022} This dataset contains 4000 entries: 3200 train and 800 validation.
elements.id-string-32: 17.4\% of the train dataset is \verb|multi|, 39.8\% of the train is \verb|passage|, and the remaining 42.8\% is \verb|phrase|.
elements.id-string-33: The dataset contains text and various metadata.
elements.id-string-34: Initial experiments found that the metadata did not help with predictions, so we do not utilize it in any predictions.
elements.id-string-35: The relevant parts of the dataset are the \texttt{targetParagraphs} column, the \texttt{targetTitle} column, the \texttt{spoiler} column, and the \texttt{tags} column.
elements.id-string-36: The \texttt{targetParagraphs} column contains the text of an article that contains the spoiler.
elements.id-string-37: In the dataset, it is formatted as a list where each element is a line of the article.
elements.id-string-38: The \texttt{targetTitle} contains the clickbait title of the article.
elements.id-string-39: The \texttt{spoiler} column contains the spoiler to the article.
elements.id-string-40: This spoiler is always a direct span of the text.
elements.id-string-41: The \texttt{tags} are the type of spoiler.
elements.id-string-42: There are three types of spoilers that we classify: \texttt{phrase}, \texttt{passage}, and \texttt{multi}.
elements.id-string-43: The \texttt{phrase} spoiler is always a span from the text less than or equal to 5 words in length.
elements.id-string-44: The \texttt{passage} spoiler is a single span of text longer than five words in length.
elements.id-string-45: The \texttt{multi} spoiler is multiple non-continuous spans of text.

elements.id-string-48: Previously, many have taken on the task of detecting clickbait, such as approaches which not only detect the presence of clickbait, but also sort out and puts into categories based on their content such as inflammatory clickbait, ambiguous clickbait, and exaggeration clickbait.
elements.id-string-49: \cite{pujahari_sisodia_2019} This method allowed for detection, but it was incapable of actually solving the clickbait issue.
elements.id-string-50: There have also been attempts to generate clickbait using NLP.
elements.id-string-51: These approaches use a summarization method to make sensationalized headlines for articles.
elements.id-string-52: \cite{xu_wu_madotto_fung} This work makes the problem worse as it removes the human aspect of creating clickbait and makes the generation of clickbait easier and quicker.

elements.id-string-60: The first task that we tackle is classification of the clickbait into the three types shown above.
elements.id-string-62: The inputs are the title of the article, and the output is one of the three types referenced above: \texttt{phrase}, \texttt{passage} and \texttt{multi}.
elements.id-string-63: We chose to only input the title because we found that the text of the article had little no no correlation with the performance of the model.
elements.id-string-65: We defined two models for this task.
elements.id-string-66: Both models are binary classifiers made using the deBERTa \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2006-03654}
elements.id-string-67: neural network model for sequence classification.
elements.id-string-68: The first model that we use classifies between the \texttt{multi} spoilers and the other types of spoilers.
elements.id-string-69: We refer to this model as Model 1 in the section hereafter.
elements.id-string-70: The second model classifies the \texttt{passage} versus the \texttt{phrase} spoiler.
elements.id-string-71: We refer to this model as Model 2 in this section hereafter.

elements.id-string-75: For both models, we sought to tune the batch size, epoch count, learning rate, and weight decay parameters.
elements.id-string-76: The batch size is the amount of samples that are passed to the model before it updates.
elements.id-string-77: The epoch count is the amount of iterations that the machine learning model goes through before the final model is trained.
elements.id-string-78: The learning rate is a parameter that determines how fast the model moves towards the optimal weigh values.
elements.id-string-79: The weight decay parameter regularizes the weights of the model to prevent overfitting.
